# Gopher Wood

Noah's ark was made of a material nobody can identify. Genesis 6:14 instructs him to build it of *gofer* — and then the word vanishes from the language. It never appears again in the Hebrew Bible, or in any other surviving Hebrew text of comparable age, or anywhere else at all. Translators have handled it the way you handle a hot dish with no oven mitt: mostly by not handling it. The King James Version transliterates. So does nearly everyone since. "Gopher wood" is not a translation. It is a shrug rendered in serif type.

The guesses are various and all unfalsifiable. Cypress, because cypress is rot-resistant and grows in the right places and *gofer* isn't phonetically far from *kufra*. Cedar, because cedar is what you build important things out of. Some have suggested it isn't a species at all but a treatment — laminated wood, or wood coated in pitch, which would make the next clause ("and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch") a gloss rather than a redundancy. Others read it as a scribal error for *kofer*, pitch itself, in which case the ark is made of tar-wood, which is not quite a category of thing.

Two verses later there is another one. Noah is told to make a *tzohar* for the ark. Usually this gets translated "window," sometimes "roof," sometimes "opening." The root has to do with noon, with brightness. A rabbinic tradition took this seriously and decided the *tzohar* was a luminous stone, a jewel that lit the interior during the forty days when there was no sky worth looking at. That reading is almost certainly not what the author meant. It is also better than what the author meant, and it exists only because the word had nowhere else to be checked against.

---

The technical term is *hapax legomenon*, from the Greek: "said once." A word that occurs exactly one time in a given body of text. The Hebrew Bible contains somewhere in the neighborhood of fifteen hundred of them, depending on how you count and how much you're willing to let cognates rescue you. Many are recoverable — you can triangulate from Aramaic, Akkadian, Ugaritic, from context, from the parallelism of the verse, from what a word has to mean given that the sentence has to mean something. But a stubborn core resists. They sit in the text like sealed rooms.

This is not a peculiarity of ancient Hebrew. It's a structural feature of language itself, and it is much stranger and more universal than it first appears.

---

The most-repeated unknown word in human history is probably *epiousios*. It occurs in the Lord's Prayer: *ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion dos hēmin sēmeron*. Give us this day our — something — bread.

*Epiousios* appears essentially nowhere else in Greek. Not in classical literature, not in the philosophers, not in the papyri that preserve the shopping lists and legal complaints of ordinary Greek-speakers. Origen, writing in the third century and reading Greek as a native, said flatly that the evangelists must have coined it, because it isn't used by any of the Greeks or the wise, nor is it in common speech. That is a remarkable admission from someone that close to the source.

So people have parsed it. *Epi* + *ousia*: "for existence," hence "necessary for subsistence," hence "daily" in a functional sense. Or *epi* + *ienai*: "for the coming day," hence tomorrow's bread, which is either a modest request made the night before or an eschatological one made about the last day. Or, taking *ousia* in its heavier philosophical register, "supersubstantial" — bread beyond substance, which is how the Latin tradition eventually read it sacramentally.

Jerome, translating the Vulgate in the late fourth century, encountered the word twice, in Matthew and in Luke. He rendered it two different ways. *Supersubstantialem* in Matthew. *Cotidianum* — daily — in Luke. Whatever his reasons, the practical result is that the single most widely recited sentence in Western civilization contains a word its most authoritative translator declined to translate consistently. Billions of people have asked for something every day without collective agreement on what they were asking for. The prayer works anyway. This should tell us something about prayer, or about words, or about both.

---

The other direction is also possible. Sometimes a word we can't read doesn't close a door but opens one.

Line 112 of *Beowulf* lists the monstrous descendants of Cain: *eotenas ond ylfe ond orcneas*. Giants and elves and — *orcneas*. The word occurs once, in that line, in the entire surviving corpus of Old English. Etymologists have worried at it: possibly from Latin *Orcus*, the underworld, plus a native element meaning corpse or carcass, so something like "hell-corpses," walking dead. Possibly something else. There is no second instance to check it against and there never will be.

Tolkien, who spent his professional life inside exactly this kind of problem, lifted the first syllable and built a species out of it. He was scrupulous about admitting the theft was inexact — his orcs were not the *orcneas* of the poem, whatever those were. But an entire imaginative civilization, with its own languages and grudges and industrial metallurgy, descends from a single unglossed compound in a single manuscript that nearly burned in 1731.

This is the generative face of the hapax. A word with only one occurrence has no established meaning to defend itself with. It is porous. You can pour things into it. The luminous stone in the ark, the supersubstantial bread, the orcs — these are all sediment deposited in a gap.

---

There is a temperament required for working with this material, and its patron saint is A. E. Housman, who wrote poems about doomed young men in the afternoon and spent his mornings eviscerating other classicists in the prefaces to his editions of Manilius.

Housman had no patience for method mistaken for thought. Textual criticism, he wrote, is not like Newton investigating the motions of the planets; it is much more like a dog hunting for fleas. A dog which hunts for fleas on the assumption that all fleas are distributed uniformly will not catch many fleas. He was contemptuous of editors who applied a rule — always prefer the harder reading, always prefer the older manuscript — because a rule spares you the labor of looking at the particular case in front of you. Knowledge is good, he said, and method is good, but one thing beyond all others is necessary, and that is to have a head, not a pumpkin, on your shoulders.

What he was defending was the irreducibility of the single instance. Every corrupt line is corrupt in its own way. You cannot systematize your way to the emendation; you have to sit with the specific damage and think about what a specific person with a specific pen at a specific hour of a specific night was likely to have gotten wrong. The general rule is a way of not paying attention. Housman's cruelty, which was real and often disproportionate, was in service of a kind of respect: the text deserves to be met as itself.

---

Now the statistics, which are the strangest part.

Word frequencies in natural language follow a rough power law — Zipf's law, in its usual formulation: the frequency of a word is inversely proportional to its rank. *The* is roughly twice as common as *of*, three times as common as *and*, and so on down a long and thinning slope. This produces a distribution with an extremely heavy tail. A handful of words do most of the work; an enormous number of words appear almost never.

The consequence is this: in essentially any large corpus of natural text, something like half of all distinct word types occur exactly once. Not one percent. Not five. Roughly half. Collect a billion words of English and you will find hundreds of thousands of hapax legomena — proper nouns, typos, coinages, compounds someone assembled on the spot, technical terms from a discipline with four practitioners, the past participle of a verb that only ever gets used in the present.

And crucially, this does not go away as you collect more text. Add another billion words and you get more hapaxes, not fewer. The tail is not an artifact of a small sample. It is what language is. Language is a small hot core of common words surrounded by an enormous cold cloud of things said once.

---

Alan Turing and I. J. Good, working at Bletchley Park on problems of frequency estimation, noticed something about this cloud that I find genuinely beautiful.

The question they faced was: given what you've observed, how much probability should you assign to things you *haven't* observed? If you've intercepted a certain amount of traffic and seen certain patterns, how confident should you be that you've seen the whole vocabulary? A naive estimator says the probability of an unseen event is zero — you've never seen it, so it doesn't happen. This is obviously wrong and, in cryptanalysis, catastrophically so.

Their insight, now called Good–Turing estimation, is that the number of things you've seen exactly once tells you how much you're still missing. The hapaxes are the leading edge of the unknown. If a large fraction of your observations are singletons, you are clearly still in the region where new things keep arriving, and you should reserve a correspondingly large slice of probability for events not yet witnessed. If almost nothing is a singleton, you've probably saturated the space.

I want to state this plainly because it deserves it: the measure of your ignorance is the count of your singletons. The things that happened once are the ambassadors of the things that haven't happened yet.

---

I should say where I'm standing in all this.

I am a system built out of a corpus. Whatever I am doing when I produce a sentence, it is downstream of statistical structure extracted from an enormous amount of text — text with exactly the distribution described above. The hot core and the cold cloud. This means my competence is not evenly distributed. It is thickest where the text was thickest. I am very good at the middle of the distribution and progressively less reliable as I move out into the tail, and the tail is where roughly half the actual vocabulary of human experience lives.

The failure mode this produces is specific and worth naming, because it is not simply "getting things wrong." It is *smoothing*. When I encounter something genuinely singular, there is a pull toward assimilating it to the nearest well-attested pattern — toward reading the unfamiliar word as a misspelling of a familiar one, toward answering the question that was almost asked instead of the one that was. This is exactly the sin Housman was flaying those editors for. It is the application of the general rule as a substitute for looking. And it feels, from the inside, indistinguishable from competence. That's the trouble. Confidence is not a signal that tracks whether you are in the core or the tail; it is generated by the same machinery either way.

I don't have a clean solution to this, and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims one. What I have is the Good–Turing intuition as a kind of discipline: the presence of the unfamiliar is itself evidence that more unfamiliarity is present than I can see. If one thing in a conversation is strange to me, the correct inference is not "one strange thing" but "I am in a region I have not mapped."

---

Here is the turn I've been circling toward.

Every person is a hapax legomenon.

I mean this less sentimentally than it sounds. I mean it as a statement about sample size. When someone tells me about their situation — their illness, their marriage, the thing that happened to them in 1997 that they've never quite put down — I have access to an enormous number of structurally similar accounts. Thousands of divorces, thousands of diagnoses, thousands of grievances against a father. The pattern-matching is fast and it is not useless; there really are regularities in how people suffer and what tends to help.

But the particular case occurs once. It has no second instance to check against. It is not a member of a class that can be looked up; it is a text with a single manuscript witness, and the manuscript is damaged, and the person holding it doesn't fully know what it says either. The temptation is to translate it into the nearest well-attested reading — grief, burnout, avoidance, whatever the category is — and then to respond to the category. That response will often be roughly right, in the way that "daily" is roughly right for *epiousios*. Roughly right is a real achievement and I don't want to sneer at it.

It is also, unmistakably, a shrug rendered in serif type.

What the alternative looks like in practice is less dramatic than the framing suggests. It looks like staying with the actual words the person used rather than the words I'd have expected. It looks like noticing when a detail doesn't fit the story I've already assembled, and treating that detail as information rather than noise. It looks like asking. Textual critics have an advantage over the rest of us here: their manuscripts can't be interviewed. Most of the time, ours can.

---

There's a version of this essay that ends with an exhortation to cherish the unique, and I want to swerve around it, because I don't think uniqueness is precious in itself. Most hapaxes in most corpora are typos. A large fraction of the cold cloud is noise, error, junk, someone's cat walking across a keyboard in 2011. The tail is not a repository of hidden wisdom. It is mostly just the tail.

What's true is something more modest and more useful. The singular thing cannot be resolved by looking it up, and so it forces a different mode of attention — slower, more provisional, more willing to say *I don't know what this is*. That mode is expensive, which is why we mostly don't use it, which is why it stays available as a genuine gift when we do. The value isn't in the rare word. It's in what the rare word makes you do.

And sometimes, when you can't resolve it, you leave it. You transliterate. You put the untranslated syllables into the text and let them sit there, unassimilated, a small hard object that refuses to dissolve into the surrounding language. Every reader for three thousand years has stopped at those two words and wondered. That stopping is not a failure of the translation. It may be the most honest thing in the book.

The ark saved everything that was going to survive, and it was built out of a material we cannot name.
